title: Prompt engineering essentials
notes: Most bad answers come from missing information, not missing magic words: be specific and give the model the facts.
Examples teach style fastest, and naming the format tells the model exactly what shape to answer in.
Break big tasks into steps, test prompts on real emails, and fix one gap at a time.

slides.title: Prompt engineering essentials
slides.sub: Five habits that turn a vague request into one the model gets right
sentences: You now know the model predicts the most likely text, given what it can see.
So the words you send are your main control over what comes back.
In this lesson you will learn five habits that make a prompt clear, and watch a vague prompt for Scout become a good one.

slides.title: Same email, two prompts

left.label: Vague prompt
points: Three wandering paragraphs, one invented promise

right.label: Clear prompt
points: Who Scout is and who is asking

sentences: Here is one customer email, sent to the same model with two different prompts.
On the left, the vague one: reply to this customer.
The model has no policy, no order details and no idea how long or how formal to be.
So it writes three friendly paragraphs, and fills every gap with whatever sounds likely.
On the right, the clear prompt says who Scout is, gives the policy that applies, and asks for two or three plain sentences with no promises.
Same model, same email, and now the answer is short and correct.
The difference is not magic words; it is information the model needed and did not have.

slides.title: Five habits of a clear prompt

note.text: The test: would a smart new colleague, on day one, know what to do?

sentences: Prompt engineering sounds technical, but it is mostly clear writing for a very literal reader.
First, be specific: say exactly what you want, not roughly what you mean.
Second, give context: the facts it needs, who the reader is, and why the task matters.
Third, show examples, because one or two good answers teach style faster than a paragraph of rules.
Fourth, name the output format: how long, what layout, and which fields.
Fifth, break big tasks into smaller steps the model can take one at a time.
A good test is to imagine handing your prompt to a smart new colleague on their first day: would they know what to do?

slides.title: Small edits, big difference

cells: Answer her return question in 2 to 3 sentences.
Policy: returns within 30 days of delivery.
Reply with one word: return, exchange or other.
First find the order number, then the request.

note.text: Each fix adds something the model could not have guessed.

sentences: Here is what those habits look like as small edits to real instructions.
Instead of help this customer, say what to answer and how long the answer should be.
Instead of hoping it knows the policy, paste in the rule that applies.
Instead of asking what she wants, list the exact answers you will accept.
Instead of handle this ticket, give the steps in order.
Every one of these edits adds something the model could not have guessed on its own.

slides.title: Show, don't just tell
slides.lead: A few solved examples before the real task. This is called few-shot prompting.

rows.code: Tag each email: where_is_order, return or other.
Email: Has my tent shipped yet?  Tag: where_is_order
Email: Boots pinch, can I send them back?  Tag: return

aside.label: Vary your examples
aside.text: Models copy examples closely, including length and wording. Use different ones so it copies the idea.

sentences: Examples are one of the strongest tools you have.
Start with the instruction: tag each email as where is order, return or other.
Then show a solved example: has my tent shipped yet is tagged where is order.
And another: boots that pinch and need sending back are tagged return.
Finally, give the new email, and the model continues the pattern.
This is called few-shot prompting: a few solved examples, shown before the real task.
Keep your examples varied, because the model copies their length and wording as well as their meaning.

slides.title: Break big tasks into steps

note.text: Small steps are easier to get right and easier to check. Later, each can be its own call.

sentences: The last habit is breaking big tasks down.
Customer emails are messy: one message can ask about an order, a return and a size, all at once.
So ask the model to first pull out the facts: the order number, the item and what the customer wants.
Then to work out which policy rule applies.
And only then to draft the reply, short and within policy.
Smaller steps are easier for the model to get right, and easier for you to check.
Later in the course, each of these steps can become its own call, or a tool.

slides.title: Prompts are tested, not just written

note.text: Keep the emails you test with. In Module 5 they become Scout's test set.

sentences: Nobody writes a perfect prompt first time, so treat it like code: write, run, read and fix.
Write the clearest first version you can.
Run it on ten or so real emails, not just the one you had in mind.
Read every answer, because the problems hide in the ones you skip.
Then fix the single biggest gap, and run the same emails again.
Changing one thing at a time tells you which change actually helped.
Keep those emails, because in Module 5 they become Scout's test set.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: Bad answers usually mean missing information, not missing magic words
Be specific, give context, show examples, name the format
Break big tasks into steps the model can take one at a time
Test on real emails and fix one gap at a time

sentences: Let us pull it together.
When the model gives a poor answer, look first for information the prompt left out.
Be specific, give context, show examples and name the format you want.
Break big tasks into steps the model can take one at a time.
And test your prompt on real emails, fixing one gap at a time.
Next, you will put these habits into the most important prompt of all: Scout's system prompt.

midQuiz.q: Scout's one-line prompt produced three paragraphs and an invented promise. What was mainly missing?
options: Polite words, like please and thank you
Information: the policy, the length and the rules
midQuiz.explain: The model filled the gaps with typical text. Giving it the facts, the length and the rules removes the gaps.
midQuiz.hint: Did the model misbehave, or did it do its best with what it was given?

midQuiz.q: Which instruction names the output format?
options: Answer in two or three sentences, with no lists.
midQuiz.explain: It tells the model exactly how long the answer should be and what layout to use.
midQuiz.hint: Look for the one that describes the shape of the answer, not who is speaking.

endQuiz.q: Both of your example replies open with "Great question!". What will the model most likely do?
options: Ignore the wording of the examples
Start its own replies with "Great question!" too
endQuiz.explain: Models copy examples closely, including wording and length, so vary your examples.

endQuiz.q: One email asks about an order, a return and a size swap. What is a good prompt strategy?
options: One instruction: handle everything in this email
Steps: pull out the facts, match the policy, then draft the reply
Ask the customer to send three separate emails
endQuiz.explain: Smaller steps are easier for the model to get right and easier for you to check.
endQuiz.hint: Think about the fifth habit on the hub slide.
